Score-based physics-informed learning framework for stochastic dynamics

abstract:
Abstract
The Fokker-Planck equation is crucial for characterizing the dynamics of stochastic systems and predicting their evolutionary behavior. In practice, the forward problem of the Fokker-Planck equation becomes ill-posed when the system dynamics and initial conditions are incompletely known. Meanwhile, the inverse problem for inferring dynamical coefficients is fundamentally constrained by the inherent unobservability of probability densities, which restricts available data to discrete-time particle observations. To address these challenges, we propose a novel Score-based Physics-informed Learning Framework that leverages score matching to connect particle observations with the forward and inverse problems of the Fokker-Planck equation, without requiring density reference solution or complete system dynamics. Experimental results demonstrate that our method achieves superior accuracy, computational efficiency, scalability to high dimensions, and robustness to data sparsity and noise.

  - heading "Introduction" [level=2]
  - text: "Stochastic dynamical systems, mathematically formulated by stochastic differential equations (SDEs), provide a fundamental framework for modeling random phenomena in physics, biology, engineering, and finance [1]. The Fokker-Planck (FP) equation characterizes the temporal evolution of the probability density function [2], playing a central role in analyzing the underlying dynamics and predicting system behavior. In reality, learning stochastic dynamics from the perspective of the FP equation faces two obstacles: (i)"
  - emphasis: the governing dynamics of system are typically incompletely known
  - text: (
  - emphasis: i.e.
  - text: ", drift and diffusion terms), and (ii)"
  - emphasis: the probability density is generally not directly measurable
  - text: ", with available data limited to particle observations at discrete time instants. From discrete-time particle observations, solving the forward and inverse problems of the FP equations,"
  - emphasis: i.e.
  - text: ", inferring dynamical coefficients and reconstructing probability densities, poses significant challenges, as shown in Fig. 1."
  - text: For the forward problem, simulation-based methods [3], [4], [5] require extensive sampling of SDE trajectory to approximate the probability density, while mesh-based methods are limited by high dimensional computational complexity [6], [7]. In recent years, deep learning-based PDE solvers have demonstrated strong potential in overcoming the curse of dimensionality [8], [9], [10], [11], [12].
  - emphasis: Physics-informed neural networks
  - text: (PINNs) have emerged as a powerful framework for solving both forward and inverse problems of partial differential equations (PDEs) by embedding physical laws into the neural network training process [12], [13], [14], [15]. Deep learning-based methods have been successfully applied to FP equations [3], [16], [17], [18], [19], [20], [21], [22]. However, all these methods rely on complete knowledge of governing equations and well-posedness conditions. Concurrently, Ren et al. [23], [24], [25], [26] pioneered a data-driven framework integrating deep learning with stochastic dynamics, which enables direct data-driven solutions to the FP equation and a broad class of related stochastic problems.
  - generic: For the inverse FP problem, PINNs rely on reference probability densities as supervisory signals. In practice, however, only particle snapshots at a few time instants are available, which makes the problem significantly more challenging. Existing methods have been developed for identifying dynamical coefficients from particle observations of stochastic system [27], [28], [29], [30], [31], [32], but fail to solve the forward problem due to the lack of initial conditions.
  - text: Several methods use observed particle data to estimate probability densities, as coarse label data to train PINNs. Kernel density estimation (KDE) [33] enables nonparametric estimation of probability densities, but incurs considerable errors when data is insufficient. An alternative approach [34] employs the variational form of the Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence [35], which demonstrates promising performance in certain low-dimensional scenarios. However, its reliance on numerical integration introduces significant computational overhead, limiting its scalability to high-dimensional problems. To address these issues, we propose a novel
  - emphasis: Score-based Physics-informed Learnig Framework
  - text: (SPLF) that bridges particle observations and FP equation solving through
  - emphasis: score matching
  - text: "[36], [37], [38]. By learning the score function in an unsupervised manner, our method circumvents the need for explicit density estimation. Experimental results demonstrate that SPLF achieves high computational efficiency in high-dimensional settings and exhibits strong robustness to both data sparsity and perturbation in the observations."
  - text: "Our contributions can be summarized as follows:"
  - list:
    - generic: •
    - strong: Score-driven unified learning framework for stochastic dynamics.
    - text: We propose a novel framework that bridges particle observations and stochastic dynamics by leveraging score matching. Without requiring explicit density estimation, the score function can be learned in an unsupervised manner from particle data, enabling a unified treatment of both the forward and inverse problems of the FP equation.
    - generic: •
    - strong: Solving the FP equation with unknown initial conditions.
    - text: The score function naturally provides a well-posedness condition for the FP equation, in the absence of initial density. Under the constraints of the score matching and FP equation, we obtain an unnormalized density that can be normalized by computing the partition function at a single time step.
    - generic: •
    - strong: Score-based formulation for dynamics identification.
    - text: We leverage a score-based FP equation that depends only on the score function and the unknown dynamical coefficients. Combined with score matching, this formulation enables the identification of system dynamics from discrete-time particle observations.
    - generic: •
    - strong: High-performance algorithm for data-physics integration.
    - text: SPLF seamlessly integrates score matching into the PINN framework to solve the forward and inverse FP equations, effectively combining observational data with physical constraints. Extensive experiments demonstrate that SPLF consistently outperforms existing methods in terms of accuracy, computational efficiency, robustness to data, and scalability to high-dimensional problems.
  - emphasis: Deep learning-based FP solvers.
  - text: "Deep learning-based methods, including Deep BSDE [8], Deep Ritz [9], [39], PINNs [12], and Neural Operators [10], [11], have emerged as promising alternatives for efficiently solving PDEs. These approaches demonstrate excellent computational efficiency and strong potential in high-dimensional scenarios, and have been successfully applied to both steady-state [3], [16], [17], [18], [19] and time-dependent FP equations [20], [21], [22]. Notably, both FPNN [19] and Score-PINN [21] leverage score function representations to effectively solve FP equations with known dynamics: FPNN targets steady-state problems and Score-PINN addresses the initial value problem for time-dependent FP equations. Boffi et al. [40], [41], [42] developed a series of methods that approximate the score function via score matching and employ it to construct the probability flow equation, enabling a deterministic transport of samples from the initial distribution to the target distribution. In contrast, our work tackles the more challenging scenario where the underlying dynamics are uncertain and initial conditions are unknown, aiming to solve both forward and inverse problems of FP equations purely from particle observation data."
  - emphasis: Data-driven methods for dynamics identification.
  - text: Data-driven approaches have achieved significant progress in the identification of complex dynamical systems. Brunton et al. [43], [44] introduced sparse regression methods for discovering deterministic dynamical systems from measurement data. For stochastic dynamics, Ruttor et al.[27] developed a non-parametric Bayesian framework based on Gaussian processes to infer the drift term. Methods based on the Kramers-Moyal formulas have been proposed in [28], [29] to identify the drift and diffusion coefficients of stochastic systems. Additionally, several studies [30], [31], [32] employed physics-informed generative models to characterize the underlying stochastic processes. These methods are effective in solving inverse problems but do not focus on forward problems.
  - emphasis: Score-based generative models.
  - text: Score matching [36], [37], [38] enables direct estimation of score functions from sample data, serving as the basis for score-based generative models [45], which establish a unified framework for noise-based generative models like SMLD [46] and DDPM [47], [48], achieving impressive generative performance in both quality and efficiency. These models can be viewed as discretizations of an underlying SDE, where a forward SDE progressively adds noise to the data, and the reverse process, described by a reverse SDE or probability flow ODE [49], [50], denoises the data based on the estimated score. Inspired by this, we employ score matching to integrate observed data for learning both the density information and the underlying dynamics. Our framework combines PINNs with score matching to address forward and inverse problems in stochastic dynamics.
